chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
title: Publicity after Town Hall
summary: Success spread by word of mouth; he says with the publicity of today's stars he would have been a millionaire.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Macho, in 1946, '47, pardon me, in 1947, you became a successs after you introduced Afro-Cuban jazz, Correct?
Okay. Now, how soon after that did you get another chance to play Afro-Cuban jazz, in a concert, at a dance or any place, do you recall?

Well, seems like everyvody just - the mouth-to-mouth publicity, because your Town Hall is a small place, maybe twenty-five-hundred / thirty-hundred, and the people - in those days, actually, we was the only one. Noro Morales ...

No, but I mean ehhh, Marcelino Guerra, I don't - Marcelino Guerra, all of those bands, the people, they was so gungry to know what we was doing that even having that tremendous publicity that the people has now; you imagine if we would have the publicity of Willie Colon and
Eddie Palmieri, all those guys. In those days I would be a millionaire.
